items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1967-02-09
items.q: I went to Papa Teo and took lessons with him for about a couple of years.

ctx.x: Can you tell us something about your training and taking lessons and so on?

Well, I started taking lessons around 9 years of age with my uncle, Wooden Joe Nicholas. He was my big influence on this jazz scene. And later on, I went to Papa Teo and took lessons with him for about a couple of years. Then Lorenzo Teo, his son. And finished up with him until around 1915. Then I started to go pro. My first gigs around New Orleans was with the Maple Leaf Band. Then Buddy Petite's Band. When Jimmy Noon left to go to Chicago, I played with Buddy Petite and several other bands around New Orleans.…

items.title: Albert Nicholas Interview, 1972-06-26
items.q: Old Papa Teo told me, don't just read your notes and the next one. No, you look ahead.

ctx.x: Because if you blow, you get tired. I wouldn't last. That's tiresome. But I'm blowing. I'm talking. I'm talking. I'm talking. I'm talking. It's down here. And I know, consciously. I don't know what happens. I know when to cut my notes to go into the next four bars or something. Because when I'm playing, I'm always thinking at least eight bars ahead. Sure of what I'm doing, I never guess on nobody's job. I don't practice. I practice at home. But when I'm playing, I'm concentrating at least eight bars ahead.…
I'll try it in there. Okay.
